m1.l1.title: Tour of the interface
m1.l1.mission: x64dbg has stopped at the first line of main. Find out where you are, what the CPU holds, and what is on the stack, without running a single instruction.

source.name: vault.c

steps.title: Everything at once
steps.say: This is what x64dbg looks like when it stops a program. It looks busy, but only four areas matter. Let's meet them one at a time.

steps.title: The disassembly pane
steps.say: This is the code, one instruction per line. The highlighted line, marked `RIP`, is the next instruction the CPU will run. It has not run yet.

gate.fallback: Not that one. Look for the row marked `RIP` on the left.

steps.success: That's the next instruction. Each row has four columns: the address, the raw bytes, the instruction, and a comment where x64dbg writes helpful notes, such as the text a string pointer points at.

steps.title: Spot the C
steps.say: main starts by calling puts to print the banner. Find the call to puts in the disassembly.

wrong.feedback: Close. This line loads the banner's address into `RCX`, ready for the call. The call itself is on the next line.
That line is part of main's setup. Look a few lines further down for the word call.
That's a call, but to printf. You want the one that mentions puts.

gate.fallback: Look for a line whose instruction is call and whose operand mentions puts.

steps.success: Right. Look at the comment on the line above it: x64dbg already shows the banner text, == PIRE VAULT ==. You just read your first assembly with help from the tool.

steps.title: The registers pane
steps.say: These are the CPU's registers right now. `RIP` holds the address of the next instruction. What address does `RIP` hold?

gate.fallback: Not quite. `RIP` sits below `R15` in the registers pane. Copy its value.

steps.success: Same address as the highlighted line. `RIP` and the highlighted line always agree.

steps.title: RFLAGS
steps.say: Flags live here, one bit each. When a step changes a value, x64dbg paints it red. Nothing is red yet because nothing has run.

gate.fallback: `ZF` is in the first row of flags, under `RFLAGS`.

steps.success: `ZF` is the zero flag. You'll watch it flip in Module 5. For now, just remember where it lives.

steps.title: The stack pane
steps.say: This is the stack, 8 bytes per row. The highlighted row is where `RSP` points. Its comment says “return to …”. What does that mean?

options.label: When main finishes, it returns to this address.
This is the address of main.
options.feedback: Close, but main's address is in `RIP`. The stack holds where to go back to afterwards.

options.label: This is a breakpoint.
options.feedback: Breakpoints don't live on the stack. Lesson 1.3 covers them.

steps.success: Someone called main, and the call left this return address on the stack. Module 3 covers this properly.

steps.title: The dump pane
steps.say: The dump shows raw memory: an address, 16 bytes in hex, and the same bytes as text. You'll use it to look at strings, buffers, and globals.
steps.action: Click some readable text in the dump

wrong.feedback: That's the hex column. The same bytes as text are on the right.
Those are zero bytes, shown as dots. Pick a row with words in it.

gate.fallback: Click the text column on the right side of the dump.

steps.success: Those are the program's strings, sitting in memory exactly as the compiler wrote them.

steps.title: The status bar
steps.say: Paused means the program is frozen and you are in control. While it runs, this says Running. The command box above it unlocks in Lesson 1.3.

gate.fallback: The yellow Paused label is at the bottom left.

steps.success: Whenever it says Paused, every value on screen is current.

steps.title: Getting lost on purpose
steps.say: Everyone gets lost in the disassembly. Scroll the disassembly until the `RIP` line is off screen, then press `*` to jump back.

gate.notReady: Scroll the disassembly first, so the `RIP` line is out of view.

steps.success: The `*` key takes you back to `RIP` from anywhere. You just earned your first key.

steps.title: Match the pane
steps.say: Drag each label onto the pane it describes.

gate.fallback: Not that pane. Think back to which pane you clicked for each idea.

steps.success: All four in the right place.
hints: Think about which pane changed color when you clicked `RIP`.
Code is top left, registers top right.

steps.title: Back to RIP
steps.say: If you scroll the disassembly away and press `*`, which line is highlighted?

options.label: The first line of the program.
options.feedback: `*` goes to where the CPU is, not where the program starts.

options.label: The line I clicked last.
options.feedback: `*` ignores your selection. It always goes back to `RIP`.

steps.success: `*` always brings you back to the next instruction.

steps.title: Running
steps.say: The status bar says Running. Can you trust the register values on screen right now?

options.label: Yes, they update live.
options.feedback: The CPU changes registers millions of times a second. x64dbg only shows real values while paused.

options.label: No. The values only make sense while the program is paused.

steps.success: Pause first, then read.

m1.l2.title: Controlling execution
m1.l2.mission: Walk through main one instruction at a time. Step over the boring calls, step into the interesting one, and escape when you fall down a hole.

source.name: vault.c

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.say: Quick check from last lesson: the highlighted line is `sub rsp,58`. Has it run yet?

options.label: Yes, it's highlighted because it just ran.
options.feedback: The highlight marks the next instruction, the one `RIP` points at. It hasn't run yet.

options.label: No, it runs when I step.

steps.success: Right. Nothing has run yet. Let's step.

steps.title: One instruction
steps.say: Press `F8` to run exactly one instruction. Keep an eye on the registers.
steps.success: `RIP` moved to the next line, and `RSP` dropped by `0x58`: `sub rsp,58` made room on the stack. A few flags changed too. Red means changed by the last step.

steps.title: Predict before stepping
steps.say: The next line is `lea rcx,qword ptr ds:[140003200]`. Before you press `F8`: which register will change, besides `RIP`? Click it.

wrong.feedback: `RIP` always changes. Which other register does this line write?
The first operand is where the result goes. Read it again: `lea rcx`, ...

gate.fallback: Click a register name in the registers pane.

steps.success: Let's check. Press `F8`.

steps.title: Check your prediction
steps.say: Press `F8` and see which register turns red.
steps.success: `RCX` is red and holds `140003200`. x64dbg even shows the text it points at: == PIRE VAULT ==. The line put the banner's address in `RCX`, ready to hand to puts. Module 3 explains why `RCX`.

steps.title: Step over a call
steps.say: This line calls puts. `F8` runs the whole call and stops on the line after it. The console under the dump is still empty. Try it.
steps.success: The console printed == PIRE VAULT ==, and `RIP` is on the next line. puts ran completely. You didn't see its code, and you didn't need to. Step over library calls you trust.

steps.title: Load the next string
steps.say: One more `F8` loads the prompt into `RCX`. The line after it calls printf.
steps.success: `RCX` now points at "Enter code: ". Next stop: the call to printf.

steps.title: The rabbit hole
steps.say: `F7` steps into calls instead of over them. `RIP` is on `call <vault.printf>`. Press `F7` and see what happens.

wrong.feedback: `F8` would step over it. This time press `F7` to go inside.

steps.success: You're inside printf: C runtime code the compiler copied into vault.exe, which calls even deeper into ucrtbase.dll. Nobody wrote it for this lesson and you don't need to read it. Landing somewhere like this by accident happens to everyone.

steps.title: Climbing out
steps.say: `Ctrl+F9` runs until this function is about to return.
steps.success: `RIP` is on printf's `ret`. You're still inside printf, one step from home.

steps.title: Home
steps.say: Now press `F8` to run the `ret`.
steps.success: Escaped. You're back in main, on the line after the call, and the console shows Enter code:. Remember the pair: `Ctrl+F9` to reach the `ret`, `F8` to come home.

steps.title: Run to cursor
steps.say: Stepping one line at a time gets slow. Click the `call <vault.check_code>` line (it's pulsing) and press `F4` to run until that line.

gate.notReady: Click the pulsing `call <vault.check_code>` line first, then press `F4`.

steps.success: The console shows Enter code: hello. Everything in between ran, including fgets waiting for input. The recording typed hello for you. `RIP` is on the call.

steps.title: Step into your own function
steps.say: This one is ours, and it decides whether the vault opens. Step into it.

wrong.feedback: `F8` would run check_code without stopping inside. Press `F7` to step in.

steps.success: You're inside check_code. Look at the top of the stack: a new row says return to vault.main+65. The call left that return address so check_code knows where to go back.

steps.title: Run
steps.say: `F9` lets the program run freely. There are no breakpoints, so it will run to the end.
steps.success: The console printed Access denied. and the status bar says the process stopped. `F9` means go. Next lesson, you'll put breakpoints in its way.

steps.title: Choose the key
steps.say: Pick the key for each situation.

questions.prompt: `RIP` is on call check_code and you want to see inside it.
questions.feedback: Into means see inside. Over means skip the inside.

questions.prompt: `RIP` is on call puts and you only care about what happens next in main.
questions.feedback: You don't want to see inside puts, so step over it.

questions.prompt: You're deep inside ucrtbase.dll by accident.
You want to skip to a line 20 instructions down.
questions.feedback: Pressing `F8` twenty times works, but there's a faster way.

steps.success: Four for four.
hints: Into = see inside. Over = skip the inside.
`Ctrl+F9` is the 'get me out' key.

steps.title: Which register?
steps.say: We're paused inside check_code on `mov eax,dword ptr ds:[<g_attempts>]`. Which register turns red after `F8`, besides `RIP`? Click it.

wrong.feedback: The destination is the first operand. eax is the low half of `RAX`.

gate.fallback: Click a register.

steps.success: `RAX`. eax is its low 32 bits, and the destination is always the first operand.

steps.title: Breakpoints win
steps.say: You press `F8` on a call, but there's a breakpoint inside the called function. Where do you stop?

options.label: On the line after the call, as usual.
options.feedback: Step over still stops at breakpoints. This catches people out in Lesson 1.3.

options.label: At the breakpoint inside the function.

steps.success: Step over still runs every line of the call, so a breakpoint inside it still fires.

m1.l3.title: Breakpoints
m1.l3.mission: Set three traps: one on a line of code, one on the "Vault opened!" message box, and one that fires the moment g_attempts changes.

source.name: vault.c

steps.title: Why breakpoints
steps.say: Last lesson you stepped and used `F4`. That works when the line you want is on screen. A breakpoint is a stop sign you can place anywhere, even in code you haven't found yet.

steps.title: A breakpoint on a line
steps.say: The pulsing line, `test eax,eax`, runs right after check_code returns its answer. Click it and press `F2`.

gate.notReady: Click the pulsing `test eax,eax` line first, then press `F2`.

steps.success: The address cell turned red. A red address means a breakpoint is set there.

steps.title: Run into it
steps.say: Now press `F9`. The program runs until it hits your stop sign.
steps.success: The console shows Enter code: hello and the status bar says INT3 breakpoint. `RIP` is on `test eax,eax`: check_code just returned, and its answer is in `EAX`.

steps.title: Read the answer
steps.say: What does `EAX` hold right now? Type it.

wrong.feedback: 1 would mean the code was right. Look at `RAX` in the registers pane: `EAX` is its low half.

gate.fallback: Find `RAX` in the registers pane. `EAX` is its low 32 bits.

steps.success: 0 means false. hello is the wrong code, so the vault stays shut.

steps.title: How it works
steps.say: A normal breakpoint secretly replaces the first byte of the instruction with CC, the `int3` instruction. When the CPU runs it, the debugger takes over and puts the real byte back. x64dbg hides the swap, so you'll never see CC in its views.

steps.title: Break on an API
steps.say: You don't know where the Vault opened! box is shown, but you know the function's name: MessageBoxA. Type bp MessageBoxA in the command bar at the bottom and press Enter.

wrong.feedback: Start with the command name: bp, then a space, then MessageBoxA.

gate.fallback: Type bp, a space, then MessageBoxA, and press Enter.

steps.success: The log says the breakpoint was set. x64dbg looked up MessageBoxA in user32.dll and put a breakpoint on its first instruction.

steps.title: Catch the message box
steps.say: Run with `F9` until you're inside MessageBoxA. Your breakpoint on `test eax,eax` is still set, so the program stops there first. That's expected: every breakpoint gets its turn.
steps.success: You're inside user32.dll, on MessageBoxA's first line. Look at `RDX` and `R8`: the message text and the title are already there. Module 3 explains why those registers.
hints: Stopped on `test eax,eax`? Press `F9` again.
The status bar names the breakpoint you hit.

steps.title: Before the box
steps.say: No message box has appeared yet. Why not?

options.label: We stopped on MessageBoxA's first instruction, before it did anything.
x64dbg hides windows while the program is paused.
options.feedback: Windows that already exist stay visible. This one hasn't been created yet.

options.label: The code was wrong, so no box will appear.
options.feedback: This run used opensesame, and main called MessageBoxA. Look where `RIP` is.

steps.success: A breakpoint on a function's first line stops before any of its work. Perfect for reading the arguments it was given.

steps.title: Find the variable
steps.say: g_attempts is a global counter. Let's stop the moment anything writes to it. First show it in the dump: click any byte in the dump, press `Ctrl+G`, type g_attempts and press Enter.
steps.action: Click the dump, press `Ctrl+G`, type g_attempts

gate.fallback: Type g_attempts in the box and press Enter.

steps.success: The dump jumped to g_attempts: four zero bytes at the top. It's an int, set to 0.

steps.title: Set a hardware breakpoint
steps.say: Right-click the first byte of g_attempts (it's pulsing) and choose Breakpoint, Hardware, Write, Dword. Dword because an int is 4 bytes.

wrong.feedback: Byte would only watch the first of the four bytes. Pick Dword.
Word is 2 bytes. An int is 4: pick Dword.
Qword is 8 bytes, more than the int. Pick Dword.

gate.fallback: Right-click the first byte of g_attempts, then Breakpoint, Hardware, Write, Dword.

steps.success: Hardware breakpoints use one of the CPU's four debug registers. They don't change any code: the CPU itself watches the address. Four is the limit, so the fifth one will fail.

steps.title: Fire it
steps.say: Press `F9`.
steps.success: It fired inside check_code, and the dump shows 01 00 00 00 in red. Notice `RIP` is one line past the `mov` that wrote it: hardware write breakpoints stop after the instruction that wrote. 0 became 1, which is g_attempts++.

steps.title: Disable one
steps.say: Every breakpoint you set lives in the Breakpoints tab. Click the `test eax,eax` row and press Space to disable it.
steps.action: Click the row, then press Space

gate.notReady: Click the breakpoint on `test eax,eax` (vault.main+65) first.

steps.success: Disabled. It stays in the list but won't stop the program. Press Space again any time to bring it back.

steps.title: Delete one
steps.say: Now click the hardware breakpoint row and press Delete.
steps.action: Click the row, then press Delete

gate.notReady: Click the hardware breakpoint on g_attempts first.

steps.success: Gone. A tidy breakpoint list saves a lot of confusion later.

steps.title: Choose the breakpoint
steps.say: For each goal, pick the kind of breakpoint.

questions.prompt: Stop when the program shows any message box.
questions.feedback: You know the function's name, not where it's called.

questions.prompt: Find out which code changes a global counter.
questions.feedback: You only know the data. Let the CPU watch the memory.

questions.prompt: Stop every time this specific line runs.

steps.success: Line, name, or data: that's the whole decision.
hints: Ask yourself: do I know the line, the function name, or only the data?
Only the data? That's a job for the CPU watching memory.

steps.title: Where is RIP?
steps.say: A hardware write breakpoint fires on `mov dword ptr [g_attempts],eax`. Which line is `RIP` on when the debugger stops?

options.label: On the `mov`.
options.feedback: Write breakpoints fire after the write is done, so the `mov` has already run.

options.label: On the line before the `mov`.
options.feedback: The CPU can't know about a write before it happens.

steps.success: Look one line up from `RIP` to find the write.

steps.title: A or W
steps.say: You set bp MessageBoxA, but the program calls MessageBoxW instead. What happens?

options.label: It fires anyway. They're the same function.
options.feedback: They're two different functions at two different addresses.

options.label: x64dbg shows an error when the program starts.
options.feedback: Setting the breakpoint worked fine. It's just on a function nobody calls.

steps.success: A and W are different functions; Module 7 explains why. For now, when an API breakpoint doesn't fire, try the other letter.

m1.l4.title: Following values
m1.l4.mission: The vault compares your code against a secret. Follow the pointers until you are looking at the secret itself.

source.name: vault.c

steps.title: What's in RCX?
steps.say: We set a breakpoint on check_code for you and ran to it. check_code receives one argument, input, and on x64 Windows the first argument arrives in `RCX`. `RCX` holds a number. Is it the text the user typed?

options.label: Yes, `RCX` is the text.
options.feedback: A register holds one 8-byte number. Text that doesn't fit in 8 bytes has to live in memory somewhere.

options.label: No, `RCX` is the address of the text.

steps.success: It's an address, because input is a pointer. Let's go and look at what it points to.

steps.title: Follow in Dump
steps.say: Right-click `RCX` and choose Follow in Dump.

wrong.feedback: `RCX` points at data, not code. Choose Follow in Dump.

gate.fallback: Right-click the `RCX` row in the registers pane, then Follow in Dump.

steps.success: There's what you typed: h-e-l-l-o, then a zero byte that ends the C string. The newline is gone because main replaced it with 0.

steps.title: Where does it live?
steps.say: Compare the dump's first address with `RSP` in the registers pane. Is the buffer close to the stack or far from it?

options.label: Far away.
options.feedback: Compare the digits: `14FE90` and `14FE40` are only `0x50` apart.

steps.success: Close. buffer is a local array in main, and locals live on the stack. You're looking at main's stack frame from inside check_code.

steps.title: The info box
steps.say: The pulsing line loads SECRET into `RDX`, right before strcmp compares it with your input. Click it, press `F4`, then look at the info box under the disassembly.

gate.notReady: Click the pulsing `mov rdx`,... line first, then press `F4`.

steps.success: The info box shows what's in memory before the instruction runs: SECRET's storage at `140005000` holds `140003250`, an 8-byte number that looks like an address. This line will copy it into `RDX`.

steps.title: Pointer to a pointer
steps.say: SECRET is a const char `*`, and the pointer itself is stored in memory. So it's a two-step trip: SECRET's storage holds an address, and that address points at the text. Press `F8` to run the line.
steps.success: `RDX` now holds `140003250`, the second step of the trip.

steps.title: Find the secret
steps.say: Right-click `RDX` and choose Follow in Dump.

wrong.feedback: This points at text. Try the dump.

gate.fallback: Right-click the `RDX` row, then Follow in Dump.

steps.success: opensesame. The secret was sitting in plain text in the program's read-only data, and you followed a pointer to a pointer to get there.

steps.title: Little-endian
steps.say: We pointed the dump at g_attempts for you. It shows 01 00 00 00, and g_attempts is a 4-byte int. What number is that?

wrong.feedback: That's what you get reading left to right. Flip the byte order.

gate.fallback: Read the four bytes from right to left: 00 00 00 01.

steps.success: 1. x86 stores the lowest byte first, so you read the bytes right to left: 00 00 00 01. This is little-endian, and you'll do it all the time.

steps.title: Practice the flip
steps.say: One more. What int is this, in decimal?

wrong.feedback: That's left to right. Flip it: 00 00 03 E8.
Close: 00 00 03 E8 is `0x3E8`. Convert that to decimal.

gate.fallback: Flip it to 00 00 03 E8, then convert `0x3E8` to decimal.

hints: Flipped, it reads 00 00 03 E8.

steps.title: Follow in Disassembler
steps.say: Values that point at code go to the disassembly instead. Right-click the pulsing return to vault.main+65 row in the stack and choose Follow in Disassembler.

wrong.feedback: It's a return address, so it points at code. Follow it in the disassembler.

gate.fallback: Right-click the row that says return to vault.main+65, then Follow in Disassembler.

steps.success: The disassembly shows main, on the line right after call check_code. That's exactly where check_code will return to.

steps.title: Back to RIP
steps.say: Press `*` to bring the disassembly back to `RIP`.
steps.success: Back inside check_code.

steps.title: Choose the follow
steps.say: Where do you follow each value?

questions.prompt: `RCX` holds the address of a string.
questions.feedback: Text is data. Data goes to the dump.

questions.prompt: A stack row commented return to vault.main+65.
questions.feedback: A return address points at code.
`RIP` always points at code: the next instruction.

steps.success: Data to the dump, code to the disassembler.

steps.title: Little-endian
steps.say: The dump shows these bytes for an int. Which number is it, in decimal?

wrong.feedback: That's left to right. Read the bytes from right to left.

gate.fallback: Read the bytes from right to left.

hints: Read the bytes from right to left.
00 00 00 2A in hex.

steps.title: One more
steps.say: And this one?

wrong.feedback: That's left to right. Read the bytes from right to left.
The 01 is the second byte, so it counts 256s.

gate.fallback: Flipped, it reads 00 00 01 00.

steps.success: 256. The second byte counts 256s.
hints: Flipped, it reads 00 00 01 00.
`0x100` in decimal.

steps.title: The pointer chain
steps.say: x64dbg's Memory Map tab lists where each part of vault.exe starts. Use it to place each half of the chain.

questions.prompt: SECRET's own storage, at `140005000`, is in:
The text it points at, at `140003250`, is in:
questions.feedback: `140003250` is after .rdata starts at `140002000` and before .data.

steps.success: Writable globals live in .data, constant strings in .rdata. Module 2 explains sections properly.

m1.l5.title: Getting to main
m1.l5.mission: This time there are no names. x64dbg stops before your code, and main is somewhere in thousands of instructions. Find it two different ways.

source.name: vault.c

steps.title: The first stop
steps.say: This is vault.exe freshly loaded. Before your program runs a single line, Windows has to set it up, and x64dbg pauses at the first chance it gets, inside ntdll.dll. That's not your code. Press `F9`.
steps.success: Next stop: the status bar says entry breakpoint, and the window title says vault.exe. This is the program's entry point. It's in vault.exe, but it still isn't main.

steps.title: Where are the names?
steps.say: Last time x64dbg showed names like main and check_code. Look at this listing: the call and the `jmp` show bare addresses like vault.`00000001400011A0`. Why?

options.label: This build has no symbols (no PDB file).
The program is encrypted.
options.feedback: The instructions decode fine. Only the names are missing.

options.label: This code is inside a DLL.
options.feedback: The title bar says vault.exe. The code is the program's own.

steps.success: Names like main come from a PDB file the compiler writes next to the program. Real targets almost never ship one, so from now on you'll often see only addresses.

steps.title: Route A: start from a string
steps.say: Here's the quick route. The program prints Enter code:, so the code that prints it must mention that string. Right-click the disassembly and choose Search for, Current Module, String references.

gate.fallback: Right-click any line, then Search for, Current Module, String references.

steps.success: The References tab lists every string the code uses, with the instruction that uses it.

steps.title: Jump to the code
steps.say: Double-click the Enter code: row. You'll land on the instruction that uses it.

wrong.feedback: That string works too, but let's follow Enter code: this time.

gate.fallback: Double-click the row whose string is Enter code:.

steps.success: Back in the CPU tab, on the `lea` that loads the string. This line is inside main.

steps.title: Find the top
steps.say: MSVC separates functions with runs of `int3` padding. The first real instruction after the padding is where the function starts. Click it.
steps.action: Click the first line of the function

wrong.feedback: That's `int3` padding between functions. Look just below it.
Look higher: find the `int3` lines, then take the first line after them.

gate.fallback: Click a line in the disassembly.

steps.success: `sub rsp,58` right after the padding. This is main.

steps.title: Mark it
steps.say: Press `F2` to put a breakpoint on main.

gate.notReady: Click main's first line, `sub rsp,58`, then press `F2`.

steps.title: Run to it
steps.say: Now `F9`.
steps.success: Paused at main, found without a single name. Route A done.

steps.title: Restart
steps.say: Press `Ctrl+F2` to restart the program and try the other route. Breakpoints stay set.
steps.success: Restarted. The system breakpoint is back, as always.

steps.title: Route B: the startup code
steps.say: Route A needs a useful string, and sometimes there isn't one. Route B always works for MSVC programs. The entry point calls a setup function, then jumps to the real startup routine. Get to the `jmp` and press `F7` on it.
steps.success: This is the C runtime's startup routine. Its real name is __scrt_common_main_seh. It's long in real programs, but you only need one call in it.
hints: `F8` three times gets you to the `jmp`. `F4` on it works too.
On the `jmp`, press `F7`.

steps.title: Imports as landmarks
steps.say: Calls into DLLs keep their names even without a PDB, because the program imports them by name. main needs argc, argv and the environment. Find the calls that fetch them; the call right after them is main. Click it (scroll down if you need to).

wrong.feedback: That call has a name, __p___argc, so it's a DLL function. main is ours, so it shows only as an address.
That call has a name, __p___argv, so it's a DLL function. main is ours, so it shows only as an address.
That call has a name, _get_initial_narrow_environment, so it's a DLL function. main is ours, so it shows only as an address.
That call has a name, _initterm, so it's a DLL function. main is ours, so it shows only as an address.
That call has a name, exit, so it's a DLL function. main is ours, so it shows only as an address.
Look for a call with no name, right after the call to __p___argc.

gate.fallback: Click a line in the disassembly.

steps.success: That's main. The startup code fetched the environment, argv and argc, put them in `R8`, `RDX` and `ECX`, and calls main(argc, argv, envp).
hints: main is your code, so it has no import name.
main needs argc. Look right after the call that fetches it.

steps.title: Three names for one place
steps.say: The same byte has three addresses. Its file offset is where it sits in the .exe on disk. Its RVA (relative virtual address) is where it sits relative to the start of the loaded image. Its VA (virtual address) is the full address in memory that x64dbg shows.

steps.title: Why disk and memory differ
steps.say: On disk, sections are packed close together, each aligned to `0x200` bytes (FileAlignment). In memory, Windows starts each section on its own `0x1000`-byte page (SectionAlignment) so it can mark code as executable and data as writable. The gaps are different, so file offsets don't match RVAs.

options.label: Nothing

Windows ignores it.
options.feedback: Then SECRET would point into nothing, and strcmp would crash.

options.label: The program crashes.

m2.l4.mission: Windows does a lot of work before main runs. Put the loading steps in order, and find the evidence for each one in x64dbg.

steps.title: The story so far
steps.say: In Module 1 you saw three stops: the system breakpoint in ntdll, the entry breakpoint in vault.exe, and main. This is the whole story around them. You'll find evidence for each part in x64dbg.

steps.title: The kernel maps the file
steps.say: When you start a program, the Windows kernel creates a new process and maps the .exe into memory using the section table you read in Lesson 2.1: each section goes to ImageBase plus its RVA. It also maps ntdll.dll into every process. Then it starts the first thread inside ntdll.

steps.title: The loader at work
steps.say: Code in ntdll called the loader now runs. It reads the import table, loads each DLL the program needs (and the DLLs those need), and fills in the IAT. x64dbg's Log tab shows each DLL as it arrives. Find user32.dll and click its line.

wrong.feedback: Look for the line that ends in user32.dll.

gate.fallback: Click the DLL Loaded line that ends in user32.dll.

steps.success: USER32.dll was in vault.exe's import list in Lesson 2.3. Here it's being loaded, along with KernelBase, win32u, and gdi32: DLLs user32 itself needs. Nobody listed those in vault.exe; the loader followed each DLL's own imports.

steps.title: Where the system breakpoint fits
steps.say: Near the end of the log: "System breakpoint reached!" Partway through loading, ntdll checks whether a debugger is attached and, if so, triggers a breakpoint. That's x64dbg's first stop, a courtesy from Windows. Was any of vault.exe's own code run before it?

options.label: No. `RIP` is still in ntdll, and the entry point hasn't run.

m3.l1.mission: Every call in a Windows x64 program hands over its arguments the same way. Learn the rule, then use it to read add and sum6 straight from their call sites.

steps.title: Remember MessageBoxA?

options.label: `RBX`
options.feedback: Close in the alphabet, but the convention skips `RBX`. Try again.

steps.title: The rule
steps.say: First four arguments: `RCX`, `RDX`, `R8`, `R9`, in that order. Every function in every 64-bit Windows program follows this rule: yours, the C runtime's, and Windows' own. Put the registers in argument order.

gate.fallback: C, D, then the numbered ones: `RCX`, `RDX`, `R8`, `R9`.

steps.success: That's the whole rule for the first four. x64dbg agrees: the Default (x64 fastcall) box under the registers now lists them as 1: rcx, 2: rdx, 3: r8, 4: r9.

`ECX` holds n, which is 3. `EDX` holds 5.

wrong.feedback: That keeps the upper half. A 32-bit write clears it.
That's what writing `CL` (8 bits) would do. `ECX` is 32 bits, and it clears the upper half too.

gate.fallback: The low 32 bits become 3, and the upper 32 bits become 0.

steps.success: `0x0000000000000003`. Zero-extended. This only happens for 32-bit writes: writing the 8- or 16-bit parts (`CL`, `CX`) leaves the rest alone.

m3.l2.title: Shadow space and stack alignment
m3.l2.mission: Almost every function starts with `sub rsp`, something. Work out where that number comes from, and you'll never have to wonder about it again.

source.name: calls.c

steps.title: The question
steps.say: You'll see lines like these at the top of functions everywhere: `sub rsp,28`, `sub rsp,38`, `sub rsp,48`. They're always 8 more than a multiple of 16 (hex 10). That isn't a coincidence. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to predict them.

steps.title: The shadow space
steps.say: Before every call, the caller must reserve 32 bytes (20 hex) right above where the return address will go. It's called shadow space, or home space. The called function may use it for anything, usually to save its four argument registers. You're paused on call calls.add. Click the four stack rows from `RSP` down that make up add's shadow space.

wrong.feedback: Start at `RSP`, the highlighted top row, and take the next four rows: `RSP`, +8, +10, +18.

gate.fallback: Click the top row (`RSP`) and the three rows under it.

steps.success: That's why argument 5 sits at `[rsp+20]` at the call: the first 20 hex bytes above `RSP` belong to the shadow space.

steps.title: Watch add use it
steps.say: Now inside add. Its first two lines save b and a into the shadow space main reserved: `mov dword ptr ss:[rsp+10],edx` and `mov dword ptr ss:[rsp+8],ecx`. Why `[rsp+8]` and not `[rsp]`?

options.label: `[rsp]` is reserved for `RAX`.
options.feedback: `RAX` doesn't get a slot. Look at the top row of the stack pane: what's there?

options.label: It's random.
options.feedback: Nothing about the stack layout is random. Look at the top row of the stack pane.

steps.success: call pushed the return address, so the shadow space starts at `[rsp+8]` from inside add. Debug builds save the arguments there so the debugger can always show them. Release builds usually don't bother.

steps.title: The alignment rule
steps.say: Second rule: right before any call instruction, `RSP` must be a multiple of 16. In hex, it ends in 0. Some instructions that move 16 bytes at once crash on misaligned addresses, so everyone agrees on this. Which of these `RSP` values are ready for a call?

gate.fallback: Some answers don't match yet. They're marked in red.

steps.success: Ending in 0 means aligned. Ending in 8 means 8 off.
hints: A multiple of 16 ends in 0 in hex.

steps.title: Where the 8 comes from
steps.say: The caller's `RSP` was aligned at its call. The call pushed an 8-byte return address, so at the first line of every function, `RSP` ends in 8. What must a function subtract to reserve 20 hex of shadow space for its own calls and be aligned again?

wrong.feedback: That reserves the shadow space, but `RSP` would still end in 8. Add 8 more.
Too much: `RSP` would end in 8 again. Try 8 less.

gate.fallback: 20 for the shadow space, plus 8 to fix the alignment.

steps.success: 28: 20 for shadow space plus 8 to fix the alignment. `sub rsp,28` is the most common line in Windows x64 code.

steps.title: scale's 38
steps.say: Here's scale. It needs shadow space for its call to add, plus room for its local doubled, so it uses `sub rsp,38`. Check the arithmetic: is 38 + 8 a multiple of 16 (hex 10)?

options.label: No.
options.feedback: Add in hex: 38 + 8 = 40, and 40 ends in 0.

steps.success: Rule of thumb: with no pushes in the prologue, the sub is always 8 more than a multiple of 10 hex. If the function pushes one register first, the sub becomes a multiple of 10 instead, because the push already moved `RSP` by 8.

gate.fallback: Some answers don't match yet. They're marked in red.

steps.success: That's the whole frame. scale reserved 38: 20 of shadow space, 4 for doubled, and padding to keep the alignment.
hints: The 38 hex bytes scale reserved are everything below the return address.
doubled is stored at `[rsp+20]` right after the call returns. The return address is the 8 bytes just above what scale reserved.

steps.title: Reading the offsets
steps.say: scale saved x with `mov dword ptr ss:[rsp+8],ecx` on its first line. Now it reads it back with `mov ecx,dword ptr ss:[rsp+40]`. Same variable, different offset. Why?

options.label: x was copied somewhere else.
options.feedback: Nothing copied it. Look at the line between the two.

options.label: It's a different variable.
options.feedback: The source has only one x. What changed between the two lines?

steps.success: 8 + 38 = 40. When `RSP` moves, every `RSP`-based offset changes. You'll do this arithmetic a lot.

steps.say: A function makes calls, needs no locals, and pushes nothing. What's its `sub rsp`?

gate.fallback: Shadow space plus the alignment fix.

steps.title: With a push

wrong.feedback: The push already moved `RSP` by 8, so it's aligned again.

gate.fallback: At entry `RSP` ends in 8. After one push it ends in 0.

hints: At entry `RSP` is 8 off. What does a push do to `RSP`?
push moves `RSP` by 8, so after one push it's aligned.

options.label: `[rsp+20]`
options.feedback: Something was pushed between the call site and the first line.

options.label: `[rsp+18]`
options.feedback: `RSP` went down, so offsets to the same slot go up.

steps.say: add makes no calls. Does it need a `sub rsp`?

Yes, every function does.

m3.l4.title: Volatile and nonvolatile registers
m3.l4.mission: shout calls puts in a loop. puts can trash half the registers, yet shout's counter survives every call. Find out where it hides and how shout keeps its promise to its caller.

source.name: calls.c

steps.title: The problem
steps.say:
This is calls.exe again, built in Release (/O2) this time. It's your first optimized code; Module 9 covers optimized code in depth, so for now look only at shout.

shout keeps i and times in registers. Then it calls puts, which uses registers for its own work. How does i survive?

steps.title: Two kinds of register
steps.say:
Any function you call may destroy the volatile registers: `RAX`, `RCX`, `RDX`, `R8`, `R9`, `R10` and `R11`. The nonvolatile ones (`RBX`, `RBP`, `RDI`, `RSI` and `R12` to `R15`) it may use too, but it must put the old value back before returning. `RSP` is always restored. So a value that needs to survive a call goes in a nonvolatile register.

Sort these.

steps.title: A new family
steps.say:
Floating-point values don't use `RCX` and friends. They travel in the XMM registers, which are 128 bits wide. A double uses the low 64 bits; a float uses the low 32.

Scroll the registers pane down below the flags and click `XMM0`.

steps.title: Guess the rule

options.label: `XMM0`
options.feedback: That's the Linux rule, where floats fill `XMM0`, `XMM1`, ... in order. Windows works by position.
